g.title: Modal verbs (1): will, would, should
g.rule:
At C2, will, would and should do much more than talk about the future.

will — typical behaviour, annoying habitsShe will sit for hours without saying a word. · He will keep interrupting! (stressed = irritation)
will — deduction about nowThat'll be the courier. (I'm fairly sure)
would — past habits, past refusalAs a child I would read under the covers. · The car wouldn't start.
would — softening opinionsI would imagine / I'd say it's too late.
should — expectation, probabilityThe results should be out by Friday.
should — after if/in case (formal), subjunctive useShould you need help, call me. · It's vital that he should be told.

ex.q: My flatmate ___ leave the lights on — it drives me mad!
ex.why: Stressed will = an irritating habit now.

ex.q: When we were kids, Dad ___ take us fishing every Sunday.
Someone at the door? That ___ be Aidos — he said he'd come at six.
___ you require further information, do not hesitate to contact us.
I ___ say that the plan is a little ambitious. (polite opinion)

ex.a: The parcel should arrive by the end of the week.

talk: Describe somebody who inspired you without ever telling you what to do. What exactly would they do or say?
Is pressure from a coach, teacher or boss ever useful? Where should motivation come from?

r.text:
Ask any of her former swimmers what made Roza Akhmetova an exceptional coach and you will get a vague answer. "She sort of believed in you before you did," one says. "She had loads of little rules and stuff," says another, "but mostly she listened."

She would arrive at the pool at sixish every morning, an hour or so before anyone else. She would never raise her voice. If a swimmer lost a race, she would ask a single question: "What did you notice?" Critics will tell you that elite sport demands pressure. Roza would have disagreed. Pressure, she believed, should come from the swimmer and nowhere else.

Her results were respectable, not spectacular: a couple of national medals in thirty years, give or take. What is remarkable is how many of her swimmers stayed in the sport as adults, somewhere in the region of seventy per cent by her club's own count.

Should you ever visit the pool, you will find her rules still pinned to the wall. The first reads: "Nobody improves while being afraid."

ex.q: How do former swimmers describe Roza's method?
Roza used to shout when a swimmer lost.
What does the writer find remarkable?
o: How many of her swimmers kept swimming as adults
The number of medals she won

ex.q: Where did Roza think pressure should come from?

l.intro: A podcast interview with a performance coach.

script.t: You've coached athletes and executives. What separates people who keep going from those who give up?
Honestly? It's rarely talent. People who last tend to have a reason that's bigger than the result — they'll train in the rain because they love the process, not the medal.
So rewards don't work?

They work for routine tasks. But for anything creative, research suggests that big external rewards can actually reduce motivation. People start doing it for the prize, and when the prize goes, so does the drive.
What would you say to a student who's lost interest in English, say?
I'd ask them to find a small win every day — one film scene understood, one conversation without switching languages. Progress you can see is the most underrated motivator there is.

ex.q: According to the coach, people who keep going usually…
o: have a deeper reason than the result

ex.q: When do external rewards work well?
The coach thinks big prizes always increase motivation.
What does he recommend for a demotivated student?

lessons.title: Reading: The coach who never shouted
Listening: A coach on what really motivates us

g.title: Noun phrases
g.rule:
Advanced writing packs a lot of information into the noun phrase.

compound nounsa parenting style, screen-time limits
noun + preposition phrasea fear of failure, the role of grandparents
noun + participlechildren raised abroad, parents working long hours
noun + to-infinitivethe decision to move, an attempt to help
possessive 's vs ofthe children's needs (people) · the end of the film (things)
hyphenated compound adjectivesa ten-year-old boy, a well-meaning parent

ex.q: Choose the most natural noun phrase.
o: a boy who is ten years old

ex.q: Parents ___ long hours often feel guilty.
Choose the correct form.
ex.why: For things, of is usually more natural.

ex.q: Her decision ___ (leave) the company surprised everyone.
Children ___ in two languages often code-switch.

ex.a: The role of grandparents is often overlooked.

talk: How far should parents protect a child from failure? Give an example from your own upbringing or somebody else's.
What is the most useful piece of feedback you have ever received, and why did it work?

r.text:
The well-meaning parent who removes every obstacle from a child's path has become a familiar figure. A forgotten sports kit is delivered to school within the hour; a disappointing mark prompts an email to the teacher. Each act is, in itself, an act of love. The cumulative outcome is less benign.

A child whose every setback is absorbed by an adult never discovers what a setback feels like, or that it passes. The first real one, a failed exam at eighteen or a breakdown in a friendship, then arrives without warning, and the reaction can be an outburst out of all proportion to the event.

The drawback of saying this, of course, is that it sounds like blame. It is not. Most over-involved parents had a far harsher upbringing themselves and are determined to do better.

What children need, the argument runs, is not less input but a different kind: honest feedback, a calm outlook, and the quiet confidence of an adult who is prepared to watch them struggle a little.

ex.q: What is the writer's view of over-protective acts?
o: Each is loving, but together they do harm

ex.q: The writer blames over-involved parents.
What may happen when a protected child meets a first real setback?
o: A reaction far too strong for the event

ex.q: What do children need, according to the text?

l.intro: A mother and a school counsellor discuss her teenage son.

script.t: I'll be honest. I emailed his maths teacher about the mark. My son was furious with me.
What was the outcome you were hoping for?
A re-mark, I suppose. He'd had a setback and I wanted to fix it. That's what a caring parent does.
It's what a caring parent wants to do. The drawback is that he never finds out he can survive a bad mark by himself.
My own upbringing was the opposite. Nobody ever asked how I was getting on. I promised myself I'd be different.
And you are. But there's a difference between input and control. What did his outburst actually tell you?
That he wants me to trust him. He said so, quite loudly.
Then that's useful feedback, even if the delivery was poor. Could you let the next problem be entirely his?
I could try. It will feel like neglect.
It won't look like neglect to him. It'll look like confidence.

ex.q: What did Gulmira do about her son's mark?
Gulmira's own parents were closely involved in her schooling.
What does the counsellor see as the drawback of stepping in?
o: The son never learns he can cope alone

ex.q: What does the counsellor suggest?
o: Leaving the next problem to her son

lessons.title: Reading: The cost of clearing the path

g.title: Modal verbs (2): can, could, be able to, may, might
g.rule:
can / could — ability, general possibilityStress can affect your sleep. · It could get cold at night.
was able to / managed to — a specific past successThe climbers were able to reach the summit. (not could)
couldn't — past inability (general or specific)We couldn't find a way down.
may / might / could have + past participle — speculation about the pastShe might have missed the bus.
could have — unrealised possibility, criticismYou could have told me!
may well / might well / could well — strong likelihoodPrices may well rise again.
might as well — no better alternativeThe last bus has gone; we might as well walk.

ex.q: After six hours, the rescuers ___ reach the injured climber.
ex.why: A specific past success: was/were able to or managed to.

ex.q: You ___ have warned me about the exam — I had no idea!
There's nothing on TV. We ___ as well go to bed.
She isn't answering. She ___ have left her phone at home. (possibility)

ex.a: They managed to finish the race despite the injury.

talk: Tell the story of a time you were able to do something you had thought impossible.
Is resilience something people are born with or something they build? Defend your view.

r.text:
At twenty-six, Daniyar Seitov was told that he might never walk unaided again. A climbing accident had left him with injuries that one surgeon described as irreversible.

"I couldn't accept it," he says. "I may have been naive, but I could not imagine a life in which I was powerless." For the first three months he could not sit up. By the sixth he was able to stand for a minute. He underestimated how slow the next stage would be, and admits that he misjudged his own patience. "There were days when I could have given up. I might well have, if my physiotherapist had been less stubborn than I was."

Resilience, he now thinks, is misunderstood. It is not a foolproof quality that some people simply possess. It is a habit of persevering through hardship one dull morning at a time.

Eighteen months after the accident he was able to walk into the hospital and thank the surgeon. He cannot climb, and may never be able to. He is, he says, hopeful about most other things.

ex.q: What was Daniyar told after the accident?
o: He could climb again in a year
He might never walk without help

ex.q: Daniyar says he judged his own patience correctly.
How does he now define resilience?
o: A quality you are born with
A habit of continuing day after day

ex.q: What can he still not do?

l.intro: A radio presenter interviews a pianist who returned to performing after an injury.

script.t: Leila, two years ago you were told you might never play again. What had happened?
A nerve injury in my right hand. I couldn't hold a cup, let alone play a scale. The doctors were honest: it may be irreversible, they said.
How did you react?
Badly. I felt powerless. I may have looked calm, but for months I couldn't even listen to music.
What changed?
A teacher of mine suggested pieces written for the left hand alone. I'd underestimated how much there was. Within a year I was able to give a small concert.
And the right hand?
It's improving. I can play simple things now. I might be able to perform with both hands next year, or I might not.
Does that uncertainty frighten you?
Less than it did. I misjudged what I needed. I thought I needed my old hand back. What I needed was to persevere with whatever I had.

ex.q: What was wrong with Leila's hand?
Leila stayed positive from the beginning.
What helped her return to performing?
o: Music for the left hand alone

ex.q: What does she say about next year?
o: She may or may not play with both hands
She will certainly play with both hands

lessons.title: Modal verbs (2): can, could, be able to, may, might

g.title: Participle clauses
g.rule:
Participle clauses add information concisely, especially in narratives. The subject is usually the same as in the main clause.

-ing — actions at the same time / reasonWalking along the ridge, we saw an eagle. · Feeling exhausted, he stopped.
having + past participle — an earlier actionHaving crossed the desert, they rested for a week.
past participle — passive meaningExhausted by the climb, she fell asleep.
after conjunctionsBefore setting off, check the weather. · When asked, he refused.
reduced relativesThe path leading to the lake was closed.

ex.q: ___ the summit, they took photos and started down.
___ by the storm, the hikers sheltered in a cave.
Before ___ (set) off, make sure your phone is charged.
Which sentence is correct?
o: Walking to the station, it started to rain.
Walking to the station, I got caught in the rain.

ex.q: The road ___ to the village was blocked by snow.

ex.a: Having lost the map, they followed the river.

talk: Describe the most physically demanding journey you have made. Use at least three different verbs of movement.
Why do people choose difficult adventures when comfortable holidays exist?

r.text:
Having planned the route for a year, we had not expected to lose the path on the second morning. Thick cloud had come down overnight, hiding every landmark. Not wanting to waste a day, we set off anyway.

By noon we were trudging through wet snow, each of us staring at the boots of the person in front. Crossing a stream swollen by rain, Marat slipped; he limped for the rest of the day, though he would not admit it. We scrambled up a slope of loose rock, crawled under a fallen tree and waded through mud that reached our knees.

Exhausted, we pitched the tents in the dark. Nobody spoke. Lying there, I decided that I would never hike again.

Woken at five by silence, I tiptoed outside. The cloud had gone. Seen from the ridge, the valley looked like a map of itself, and the path we had lost ran clearly along the opposite side.

Marat strode over, his limp forgotten. "Same time next year?" he said.

ex.q: Why did the group lose the path?
Marat complained loudly about his leg.
What did the writer decide in the tent?
What could they see in the morning?

l.intro: A traveller describes the hardest day of her trip.

script.t: You cycled from Almaty to Istanbul. What was the toughest moment?
Day forty, in the desert. My back wheel broke, and having been warned there were no villages for eighty kilometres, I panicked.
What did you do?
I pushed the bike — well, trudged, really — for six hours. Then a truck driver stopped. He couldn't speak English and I couldn't speak Turkmen, but we were able to fix the wheel together with wire.
Would you do it again?
Absolutely. I might well have given up that day if he hadn't stopped. But that's what I learnt: you can't plan everything — sometimes strangers are the plan.

ex.q: What happened on day forty?
How did she move for six hours?
Elena and the driver had a language in common.
What lesson did she learn?
o: Strangers can be part of the solution.

lessons.title: Reading: Four days on the ridge
Listening: A cyclist's journey across Central Asia

3A.title: Live your age
words: The information discovered as the result of research
The findings were published last month.
The findings of the study surprised everyone.
A group chosen to represent a larger group
The sample included two thousand adults.
They tested a sample of 500 teenagers.
Large enough to be important; not likely to be by chance
There was a significant difference between the two age groups.
A connection between two things, not always cause and effect
Researchers found a strong correlation between sleep and mood.
a correlation between A and B
There is a correlation between age and income.
An idea that is tested by research
We need to test this hypothesis.
To organise and carry out research or a survey
The study was conducted in five countries.
They conducted a survey of retired people.
Checked by other experts before publication
The article appeared in a peer-reviewed journal.
A person who takes part in a study or activity
All participants in the study were over sixty.
Facts or numbers collected for analysis
The data suggest that people become happier after fifty.
The data show a clear trend.
Something that can change and affect a result
Income was the most important variable.
They controlled for the age variable.

g.title: Determiners: articles and quantifiers
g.rule:
zero article — general plural/uncountableOlder people tend to sleep less. · Research shows…
the + adjective — groupsthe elderly, the young, the unemployed
a / an with uncountables in a specific sensea good education, a knowledge of history
quantifiers + of + the/possessivemost of the participants, none of my friends
few / a few, little / a littleFew people knew (= almost none). · A few people knew (= some).
every / each, either / neitherEach participant was tested. · Neither result was significant.

ex.q: ___ elderly are often more satisfied with life than young adults.
___ research suggests that happiness rises after fifty.
Very ___ people realised the study had been flawed. (almost none)
___ of the two groups showed any improvement. (not one, not the other)
She has ___ excellent knowledge of statistics.

ex.a: Most of the participants were over sixty.

talk: Do you expect to be happier at sixty than you are now? What would your answer depend on?
Describe a piece of research you have read about. How reliable did it seem, and why?

r.text:
Few claims are repeated as confidently as the idea that people grow happier with age. A good deal of research appears to support it, but the evidence deserves a closer look.

Most studies ask a sample of adults to rate their satisfaction and then compare the answers by age. The findings often show a dip in the forties and a rise afterwards. There is, however, little agreement about the cause. A correlation between age and contentment tells us nothing about why either changes.

Several variables complicate the picture. Neither income nor health is evenly distributed, and each affects mood. Some participants drop out of long studies, and those who remain may be the more fortunate. Hardly any of the surveys were conducted in more than a few countries.

None of this means the hypothesis is flawed. It means the data are not yet conclusive. The honest summary is that many people report feeling better in later life, that a significant minority do not, and that every headline on the subject should be read with some caution.

ex.q: What do many studies show?
o: A dip in the forties, then a rise

ex.q: The text says the cause of the pattern is well understood.
Why might long studies give too positive a picture?
o: Less fortunate participants may drop out

ex.q: What is the writer's conclusion?
o: The evidence is not yet conclusive

l.intro: Two researchers discuss a study on a radio science programme.

script.t: Your study claims people become happier after their fifties. How big was the sample?
Just over forty thousand adults in twelve countries, followed for ten years. The pattern is a U-shape: satisfaction dips in middle age and rises again.
Some critics say the finding is flawed — that unhappy people simply die earlier.
That's a fair point, and we did control for health. The correlation remained significant even among people in good health.
So what explains it?
We can't be certain — correlation isn't causation. But a likely factor is expectations: older people tend to compare themselves less with others.

ex.q: How many adults were in the study?
What shape describes the pattern?
The researcher completely rejects the critics' point.
What factor does he suggest?

lessons.title: Reading: Does life really begin at sixty?
Listening: Do we really get happier with age?

wear your heart on your sleeve
He wears his heart on his sleeve, so you always know his mood.
wear your heart on your sleeve
She doesn't wear her heart on her sleeve.
The decision made the club a laughing stock.
become / make somebody a laughing stock

My glasses have vanished into thin air.

A result that is certain before it happens
With their best player injured, the result was a foregone conclusion.
Her promotion was a foregone conclusion.

too much of a good thing

be too much of a good thing
You can have too much of a good thing.

She thinks he's perfect. Well, love is blind.

g.title: Word order
g.rule:
fronting for emphasisStrange it may seem, but it's true. · This I cannot accept.
inversion after negative adverbialsNever had the audience heard such language.
object + particle with pronounsTurn it off. (not turn off it)
adverbs of frequency with modal/auxHe has always loved Shakespeare.
long objects moved to the endShe explained to the class what the play was really about.
indirect questionsDo you know what time it starts? (not what time does it start)

ex.q: Choose the correct order.
o: Can you tell me where is the theatre?
Can you tell me where the theatre is?

ex.q: Choose the correct sentence.
Rarely ___ a play so moving.
She has ___ (always / admire) his sonnets.
Choose the more natural sentence.
o: He explained what the soliloquy meant to us.
He explained to us what the soliloquy meant.

ex.a: Never had the audience heard such language.

talk: Which idioms in your own language come from a famous writer or book? Explain two of them in English.
Should schools still teach four-hundred-year-old plays? Argue for or against.

r.text:
Rarely does an English speaker get through a day without borrowing from a playwright who died four centuries ago. Tell a nervous colleague to break the ice at a party, complain that a search was a wild-goose chase, or call a result a foregone conclusion, and you are using phrases that are commonly traced to Shakespeare's plays.

So thoroughly have these expressions entered the language that few people notice them. Seldom do we stop to ask why jealousy should be a green-eyed monster, or why somebody in difficulty is in a pickle.

It is worth being cautious, though. Not all of these phrases were necessarily invented by him. What is certain is that the plays are where many of them were first written down, and it is through the plays that they spread.

Nor is knowing their origin the be-all and end-all. What matters for a learner is tone. Most are informal and faintly humorous. Used well, they make speech sound natural. Used in every sentence, they are too much of a good thing.

ex.q: What is the main point of the first paragraph?
o: Shakespeare's plays are hard to read
Everyday English is full of phrases linked to Shakespeare

ex.q: The writer is certain Shakespeare invented all these phrases.
What should a learner pay most attention to?
o: The play each phrase comes from

ex.q: What happens if you use these idioms in every sentence?

l.intro: Two members of an amateur theatre group argue about their next production.

script.t: Right. The play runs for three and a half hours. Never have I seen an audience stay awake that long.
You can't cut Shakespeare. The whole town will make us a laughing stock.
On the contrary. Only by cutting will we get anybody under thirty through the door.
So what goes? Not my speech in the second act, I hope.
Not only does your speech stay, it moves to the opening. It breaks the ice beautifully.
Then I withdraw my objection. What about the costumes? Tights, I suppose.
Modern dress. Rarely does a ruff improve an actor's performance.
My mother has a heart of gold, but she will say it isn't proper Shakespeare.
Your mother came to the last one and left at the interval. Little did she know she missed your best scene.
Fine. Two hours, modern dress. But if it's a disaster, it was your idea.

ex.q: Why does the director want to cut the play?
o: It is too long for the audience

ex.q: The actor's speech is going to be removed.
Why does the actor stop objecting?
o: His speech is moved to the opening

ex.q: What will the actors wear?

lessons.title: Reading: Speaking Shakespeare without knowing it
Listening: To cut or not to cut

g.title: Cause and effect
g.rule:
verbsToy marketing leads to / results in / gives rise to stereotypes. · Stereotypes stem from / arise from early experiences.
nounsThe root cause of… · a consequence of… · has an impact on…
linkersOwing to / due to + noun · consequently, as a result, thereby + -ing
trigger / bring about / promptThe report prompted a debate. · The law brought about real change.

Note: result in (cause → effect) but result from (effect ← cause).

ex.q: Gender stereotypes often stem ___ the toys children play with.
The campaign resulted ___ a 20% rise in applications.
The match was cancelled ___ to heavy rain.
The new policy ___ about a major change in hiring.
They lowered prices, ___ attracting new customers.

ex.a: The report prompted a national debate.

talk: What are the pros and cons of treating boys and girls in exactly the same way at school?
Describe one way in which your childhood has affected the adult you are. What caused what?

r.text:
A primary school in a northern town has spent a year trying to remove gender from its classrooms, and the results have given rise to a lively argument.

The experiment stemmed from a teacher's observation. Asked to describe themselves, the girls in her class chose words about appearance, while the boys chose words about strength. Since the children were only seven, she concluded that the difference was learned.

Consequently, the school changed a great many small things. Coat pegs were no longer colour-coded. Teachers stopped saying "boys and girls" and, owing to a new rule, praised every child for effort. Books were chosen so that adventurers and carers appeared, by and large, in equal numbers.

The pros and cons are still being weighed. Some parents are sick and tired of what they see as interference. Others report that their sons now talk more readily about feelings, which has led to calmer homes.

First and foremost, the head teacher says, the aim was choice. "Sooner or later every child meets a stereotype. We wanted them to meet it late."

ex.q: What prompted the experiment?
All the parents support the changes.
What have some parents noticed in their sons?
What was the main aim, according to the head teacher?
o: Equal numbers of boys and girls

l.intro: A married couple are shopping for their niece's birthday.

script.t: Why is everything on this side pink? I only want a building set.
Because of marketing. Shops found that separate aisles resulted in parents buying two of everything.
So it's not that girls prefer pink?
By and large, small children don't care. The preference stems from what they see around them.
My sister says Amina only wants dolls.
Which may be due to the fact that nobody has ever given her anything else. That's cause and effect, not nature.
All right. The building set, then. Although she'll be sick and tired of it in a week.
Possibly. Children work things out by trial and error. Hence the receipt.
And the wrapping paper? There's only pink or blue.
Brown paper, and she can draw on it herself. Sooner or later somebody has to give that child a choice.

ex.q: What does Yerbol want to buy?
Asem thinks girls are born preferring pink.
According to Asem, why do shops separate the aisles?
How will they wrap the present?

lessons.title: Reading: The classroom with no pink and no blue
Speaking: No more boys and girls

g.title: Aspect: perfect and continuous tenses
g.rule:
Perfect aspect looks back from a point (completion, result, time up to now). Continuous aspect shows activity in progress, duration or temporariness.

present perfect simple — result, numberI've answered forty emails today.
present perfect continuous — activity, durationI've been answering emails all morning.
past perfect continuous — background durationShe had been working there for years when she quit.
future perfect / future continuousBy 2030 I'll have paid off the loan. · This time tomorrow I'll be flying.
stative verbs rarely continuousI've known him for years. (not been knowing)

ex.q: I'm exhausted — I ___ all day.
She ___ three reports this week.
By the end of the year, we ___ (open) five new offices.

ex.a: This time next week I will be lying on a beach.

talk: Would a four-day week work in your profession or school? What would have to change?
Describe how your attitude to work or study has been changing over the last few years.

r.text:
For eleven years Saule Bekova had been answering emails at midnight. She had risen from PA to head of HR, she had never missed a KPI, and she was, by her own account, exhausted.

The change came by accident. Her company had been considering a shorter week for some time, and she was asked to run the trial. "I had been telling other people to rest for a decade," she says. "I had never done it myself."

Six months later, the figures surprised her. Output had not fallen. Staff were taking fewer sick days, and applications for jobs had doubled. By the time the AGM comes round, the scheme will have been running for a full year, and the CEO is expected to make it permanent.

Not everything has gone smoothly. Some managers have been working on their day off, and one department has quietly returned to the old hours.

Saule herself has been learning to paint. "I'm not very good," she says. "FYI, that is the whole point. Nobody is measuring it."

ex.q: What was Saule's working life like before?
Output fell during the trial.
What problem has appeared?
o: Some managers work on their day off

ex.q: Why does Saule enjoy painting?
o: She is very good at it

l.intro: A manager and an employee discuss a trial at their company.

script.t: So, six months into the four-day-week trial — what's the verdict from HR?
By and large, positive. Productivity hasn't dropped; in fact our main KPI, customer satisfaction, has gone up slightly.
And sick days?
Down by almost a third. People have been coming in rested. The cons? Some clients expect replies on Fridays, so we've had to rota a small team.
Will the CEO make it permanent?
The board meets in March — that's TBC. But I'd be surprised if they reversed it. Staff turnover has fallen too, which saves a fortune in recruitment.

ex.q: What happened to productivity?
o: It stayed the same or improved.

ex.q: By how much did sick days fall?
What was one disadvantage?
The decision to make it permanent has already been made.

lessons.title: Listening: Can a four-day week work?

g.title: Prepositions and sentence patterns
g.rule:
adjective + prepositionapprehensive about, resentful of, indifferent to, overwhelmed by
verb + object + prepositionShe accused him of lying. · They congratulated us on winning.
preposition + -ingShe left without saying goodbye. · Instead of complaining, act.

ex.q: She was apprehensive ___ moving abroad.
He seemed completely indifferent ___ the news.
They accused the manager ___ ignoring complaints.
She left the room without ___ a word.
What are you so anxious ___?

ex.a: It is only natural to feel nervous before an exam.

talk: Describe a week in which your emotions changed sharply. What were you apprehensive about, and what surprised you?
Is it better to show strong emotions at work or to hide them? Give reasons.

r.text:
On Monday I was apprehensive about the meeting, and by Tuesday I had every reason to be. My manager, on whom I had always depended for support, announced that our department was to close.

What surprised me was my reaction to the news. I had expected to be devastated. Instead I was indifferent, then faintly elated, as if a door I had been leaning on had suddenly opened. It was my colleagues who were dismayed, and I felt guilty about not sharing their distress.

By Wednesday the mood had turned. I was resentful of the directors, exasperated by the vague emails, and bewildered by how quickly ten years could be reduced to a box of belongings.

On Thursday an old friend offered me a job for which I was barely qualified. I was overwhelmed with gratitude and, an hour later, with doubt.

I accepted on Friday. Looking back, what I am most wistful about is not the job but the certainty. I am not ecstatic. I am, cautiously, content with the decision.

ex.q: How did the writer first react to the news?
The writer's colleagues were pleased about the closure.
How did the writer feel about the job offer?
What does the writer miss most?

l.intro: Backstage, a singer talks to her manager just before a concert.

script.t: I can't go on. I'm not nervous, I'm terrified. What I'm afraid of is the first note.
You were apprehensive about the last tour as well, and you were ecstatic by the second song.
That was different. I wasn't responsible for the whole evening then.
Listen. The audience are already on your side. They're not interested in finding fault.
My mother is in the third row. She's indifferent to music and devoted to criticism.
Then sing to the fourth row. What are you really worried about?
Disappointing people. I'd be devastated if they felt they had wasted their money.
Nobody has ever asked for it back. I was overwhelmed by the messages after the last concert.
You're just saying that to calm me down.
I'm capable of lying, but not that well. Two minutes. Are you ready?
No. But I'm resigned to it. Give me the microphone.

ex.q: How does the singer feel at the start?
The singer was calm before her last tour.
What is she really worried about?
What does she do in the end?

g.title: Advanced structures for comparing and contrasting
g.rule:
the … the …The longer you live abroad, the more you notice home.
modifiersconsiderably / far / a great deal more formal · nowhere near as polite · not nearly as direct
contrast linkerswhereas / while + clause · unlike + noun · as opposed to · by contrast
concessionMuch as I love Italy, … · Although / Even though … · Despite / In spite of + -ing / noun
similaritySimilarly, … · likewise · just as … so …

ex.q: ___ more you travel, the more tolerant you become.
British English is ___ near as direct as Dutch.
___ the British, Kazakhs often greet everyone in the room.
___ I admire their punctuality, I find it a little rigid.
In Japan, bowing is common, ___ in Russia people usually shake hands.

ex.a: The longer you stay, the harder it is to leave.

talk: Compare two places or cultures you know well. Use at least three different structures for contrast.
Is it possible to belong fully to two cultures at once? What is gained and what is lost?

r.text:
The Omarov family have lived in two countries for twenty years, and their children offer a neat study in contrast.

The elder daughter, born before the move, considers herself a native of her parents' city. Her younger brother, on the other hand, was born abroad and integrated effortlessly. Whereas she spoke her heritage language at home by choice, he had to be persuaded. Much as he loves his grandparents, he says, he is nowhere near as fluent as she is.

The parents, by contrast, never fully assimilated. They belong to a close-knit expatriate community, which is both a comfort and, their son suspects, a barrier. The longer they stayed inside it, the less they needed the local language.

Neither child fits the stereotype of the migrant torn between two worlds. If anything, they are amused by it. The daughter describes herself as "not so much divided as doubled".

Unlike their parents, both expect to move again. The diaspora, they point out, is nothing like as fixed as people imagine.

ex.q: How do the two children differ?
o: The son speaks the heritage language better

ex.q: The parents assimilated completely.
What does the son think about the expatriate community?
o: It may be a barrier as well as a comfort

ex.q: How does the daughter describe herself?

l.intro: Two people discuss coming home after years abroad.

script.t: Everyone warns you about culture shock abroad. Nobody warned me about coming home.
Reverse culture shock! I felt it after Spain. The longer I'd been away, the stranger everything seemed — even queuing.
Exactly. In London people apologise constantly, whereas here we're more direct. At first I found it almost rude — my own culture!
And friends weren't nearly as interested in my stories as I expected. That made me feel quite resentful, honestly.
Much as I love being back, I miss being anonymous. Here everyone knows your business.
It took me about a year to feel content again. You end up somewhere in between — not fully either.

ex.q: What surprised Arman?
How does Arman compare London and home?
o: People at home are more direct.

ex.q: Why did Sofia feel resentful?
o: Friends weren't very interested in her stories.

ex.q: Sofia felt completely settled within a month.

lessons.title: Advanced structures for comparing and contrasting

g.title: Position of adverbs
g.rule:

end (manner, place, time)He fixed it carefully in the garage last night. (manner → place → time)

ex.q: Choose the correct sentence.

Choose the correct order.
o: He repaired it last night carefully.
He repaired it carefully last night.

talk: Describe something that was made by hand and that matters to you. Who made it, and how?
Which traditional skill in your country is most likely to disappear? Should anybody try to save it?

r.text:
Aigul Nurlanovna has been weaving carpets by hand for fifty years. She almost never uses a pattern. She simply sits down at the loom each morning and, slowly, the design appears.

Her granddaughter, who works in software, is fully aware of the irony. "I assemble things nobody can touch," she says. "She makes things that will probably outlast us both."

It would be easy to be sentimental about this. Machine-made carpets are widely available and cost a fraction of the price. It is virtually impossible to earn a living at the loom, and Aigul has clearly never tried to. She sells perhaps three carpets a year.

Yet the craft is deeply rooted here, and it is highly unlikely to vanish entirely. Young people have recently begun to visit her workshop. A few carve wood or stitch leather themselves; most are just curious.

She is not bitterly disappointed that none of them stays. "They always photograph my hands," she says. "Then, occasionally, one comes back without a phone."

ex.q: How does Aigul work?
Aigul earns a good living from her carpets.
What does the granddaughter find ironic?
o: She earns less than her grandmother
She makes things nobody can touch

ex.q: Who has started visiting the workshop?

l.intro: A visitor brings a broken radio to a volunteer repair evening.

script.t: I'm probably wasting your time. It's an old radio, and it suddenly stopped working last week.
You're certainly not wasting it. Let's open it up. It was clearly assembled by hand. Look at these joints.
My grandfather bought it. I've always wanted to keep it going.
Fortunately, they made these to be repaired. A modern one is virtually impossible to open without breaking it.
Is the problem serious?
I honestly don't think so. This wire has simply come loose. Somebody has obviously stitched it together with tape before.
That would be my father. He was bitterly disappointed when it failed again.
He was nearly right. It only needs soldering properly. Can you hold this gently?
Like this? I've never done anything practical in my life.
You're doing it perfectly well. There. Turn it on slowly.
It works! I was fully aware it was hopeless, and it works.

ex.q: What has the visitor brought?
The volunteer says modern radios are easy to open.
What was wrong with the radio?
Who had tried to repair it before?

lessons.title: Reading: The last weaver on the street

6B.title: It all adds up

g.title: Singular and plural agreement
g.rule:
collective nouns (BrE)The team is / are training. (singular = unit; plural = members)
always pluralThe police are… · People were… · Cattle graze…
uncountable, look pluralThe news is… · Mathematics is… · Economics is…
amounts as one unitTen kilometres is a long way. · Five thousand tenge isn't much.
a number of / the number ofA number of students are… · The number of students is…

ex.q: Mathematics ___ my favourite subject.
The police ___ investigating the accident.
Twenty minutes ___ not long to wait.
The number of users ___ (have) doubled.
A number of people ___ complained.

ex.a: Each of the answers is worth two points.

talk: Describe a time when a number or statistic misled you or somebody you know.
Should everybody have to study statistics at school? Why, or why not?

r.text:
The news is full of figures, and a number of them are almost meaningless. Consider a headline claiming that a risk has doubled. If the odds were one in a million, they are now two in a million. The majority of readers, understandably, remember only the word "doubled".

Percentages cause similar trouble. A price that rises by fifty per cent and then falls by fifty per cent does not return to where it started; it ends up a quarter lower. Neither of the two changes is misleading on its own. Together they are.

Averages are no safer. If nine people earn a modest salary and one earns a fortune, the average tells you about nobody. Statistics is a useful subject, but everyone who uses it has to ask what has been left out.

Then there is false precision. A survey of a few dozen people reported to two decimal places sounds scientific. Approximately a third would be more honest.

The remedy is dull: ask what the figure is a fraction of. Ten minutes of school mathematics is usually enough.

ex.q: What is the problem with "the risk has doubled"?
o: It hides how small the risk may be

ex.q: A 50% rise followed by a 50% fall returns a price to its starting point.
Why can an average be misleading?
o: One very large figure can distort it

ex.q: What does the writer recommend?
o: Asking what a figure is a fraction of

l.intro: A science podcast about famous number mistakes.

script.t: Today: tiny numbers, huge consequences. Daniel, you collect maths mistakes.
I do! My favourite is a bridge that was built from both banks at once. One side used a reference height that differed by about half a metre, and the error was doubled instead of corrected.
So the two halves didn't meet?
Not at first — they were nearly a metre apart. Then there's the case of a medicine dose where a decimal point was in the wrong place: ten times the amount.
Frightening. What's the lesson?
Mathematics is rarely the problem; communication is. A number of disasters happen because two teams each assume the other has checked.

ex.q: What went wrong with the bridge?
How far apart were the halves at first?
What caused the medicine error?
o: a decimal point in the wrong place

ex.q: Daniel thinks most disasters are caused by bad maths.

lessons.title: Reading: Why nobody understands the numbers

talk: Summarise a crime story, real or fictional, using passive reporting forms (is thought to…, is said to have…).
Is prison an effective deterrent? What alternatives would you support, and for which offences?

r.text:
The case of the Aldermoor manuscript, an invented mystery, has all the elements of a classic whodunnit.

The document is thought to have been removed from the library some time in March, although the theft was not discovered until June. It is believed to have been taken by somebody familiar with the building, since no lock had been forced. A junior archivist was reported to have been seen leaving late on several evenings. He was held in custody for two days and released without charge.

Suspicion then fell on a collector, who was alleged to have offered the manuscript for sale abroad. He was convicted on the evidence of a single email and sentenced to three years. The verdict was widely felt to have been unsafe, and on appeal he was acquitted.

The manuscript is now understood to have been misfiled. It was found last year in a box labelled "maps", where it appears to have been lying all along.

Nobody was fined. The library is said to be reviewing its catalogue.

ex.q: When was the disappearance noticed?
The junior archivist was charged with theft.
What happened to the collector on appeal?
Where was the manuscript in the end?
o: In the wrong box in the library

l.intro: Two hosts discuss an unsolved museum theft.

script.t: So, the painting vanished from the gallery overnight. No alarm, no broken glass.
Which is why the police think it must have been taken by someone with a key. The night guard was questioned for hours.
And released without charge. It's now believed that the frame had been replaced weeks earlier with a copy.
Meaning the original might already have been sold before anyone noticed. If it's ever recovered, the thief is expected to face at least ten years.
Unless he's acquitted. The defence will argue that nobody can prove when the swap happened.
It's time we heard from our listeners — who do you think did it?

ex.q: How did the thief probably get in?
The night guard was charged with the crime.
What is now believed?
o: The painting was a copy all along.
A copy had replaced the original weeks earlier.

ex.q: What will the defence argue?
o: Nobody can prove when the swap happened.

7B.title: Alone or with friends?

g.rule:

I ___ wondering if you could lend me your notes.
I'd rather you ___ (not / mention) it to anyone.
Headline: "Local woman ___ lottery twice"
I ___ phone you, but my battery died.

ex.a: If only I had more time to read.

talk: Would you rather live alone or with other people? Explain what you would miss in each case.
Choose a pair of words with opposite connotations (for example thrifty and stingy) and describe a person both ways.

r.text:
I wish people would stop asking whether I mind eating alone. It's high time we separated two ideas that the language already keeps apart: solitude and loneliness.

I have lived by myself for six years. My friends would rather I didn't; they imagine evenings of silence. Suppose they visited on an ordinary Tuesday. They would find me reading, cooking something elaborate, and entirely content. I am sociable by nature, not aloof. I simply recover in quiet.

Connotation does a great deal of work here. A man alone at a restaurant is "independent"; a woman is assumed to have been let down. Call me self-sufficient and it is praise. Call me a loner and it is a diagnosis.

None of this is to deny that loneliness is real. I'd sooner admit that there are Sundays when I wish I had somebody to disagree with. If only solitude could be switched off at will.

But it's time my relatives accepted the difference. Being reserved is not being sad. I have a table for one, and I chose it.

ex.q: What does the writer want people to separate?
The writer says they are unfriendly by nature.
What does the writer say about connotation?
o: The same situation is judged differently depending on the word

ex.q: What does the writer admit?
o: Regretting the decision to live alone

l.intro: Two old friends discuss whether one of them should take a lodger.

script.t: I've been thinking of renting out the spare room. It's time I had some company.
You? You've lived alone for ten years and loved it.
I've loved the solitude. Lately it's turned into something closer to loneliness.
I'd rather you got a dog. A lodger will leave dishes in your sink.
I'm not as stubborn as you think. Determined, perhaps.
You once moved a guest's shoes because they weren't parallel. Suppose he played the drums?
Then I'd wish I had listened to you. But I'd sooner try and fail than sit here wondering.
Fair enough. What sort of person are you looking for?
Sociable but not nosy. Somebody who's curious about the world and reserved about my post.
If only such people existed. It's high time you lowered your standards.
I wish you wouldn't say that. You're my reference.

ex.q: Why does Ruslan want a lodger?
o: He has begun to feel lonely

ex.q: Karina thinks a lodger is a good idea.

talk: Describe a meal that mattered in a relationship, your own or somebody else's. What would have happened otherwise?
Which food from your country is an acquired taste? How would you persuade a visitor to try it?

r.text:
Had my grandmother been a better cook, my grandparents might never have married. This is the family legend, and I repeat it on the understanding that nobody checks the details.

They met at a neighbour's table. She had made the soup. It was, by every account, bland beyond description. The other guests nibbled politely at their bread. My grandfather, who was ravenous after a day in the fields, polished off three bowls and asked whether there was more.

She assumed he was mocking her. But for the neighbour's intervention, she would have left. Provided he apologised, she said, she might speak to him again. He did not apologise; he explained that he had no sense of taste, having lost it as a child.

Supposing he had been able to taste it, would he have lied? He always said not. As long as she cooked, he ate with enthusiasm, and whether or not the food was good remained, for sixty years, beside the point.

She eventually became an excellent cook. He never knew.

ex.q: What was the soup like?
The grandmother was pleased when he asked for more.
Why did the grandfather enjoy the soup?
What is the irony at the end?
o: She became a fine cook, but he could not tell
He learned to cook better than her

l.intro: A chef and a food writer talk about food and relationships.

script.t: They say the way to someone's heart is through their stomach. As a chef, do you believe it?
Provided the cooking is honest, yes. The first meal I made for my wife was a disaster — I burnt the rice. But for her sense of humour, we'd never have had a second date.
So it wasn't the food that won her over!
Not that night. But food is about attention. If you notice someone sipping their tea slowly, savouring it, you learn what they love.
And acquired tastes?
Ah — she couldn't stand kumis when we met. Had you told me she'd be drinking it every morning ten years later, I wouldn't have believed you.

ex.q: What went wrong at the first meal?
Why was there a second date?
According to the chef, food is about…
His wife loved kumis from the start.

g.title: Adjective order
g.rule:
Before a noun, adjectives usually follow this order (you rarely need more than three):

opinion → size → age → shape → colour → origin → material → purpose → NOUN

examplea beautiful small antique round Persian silk rug
more naturala lovely old wooden table · huge black boots
commasbetween adjectives of the same type: a cheerful, friendly waiter
after the noun / verbThe view was breathtaking. · something unusual

ex.a: She bought a beautiful old Italian painting.

talk: Describe a picture, building or view that you know very well, as precisely as you can. Mind the order of your adjectives.
Tell about a time you looked at something familiar and suddenly saw it differently.

r.text:
A small, dark, rather ordinary oil painting hung in my aunt's hall for forty years. Visitors glanced at it and walked on. It showed a narrow wooden bridge over a grey northern river, and nobody had ever stared at it for long.

After she died, I took it to a restorer, a brisk elderly woman with an enormous old brass magnifying glass. She peered at one corner for a full minute. "Somebody has painted over this," she said.

It took three months. When I returned, I could just make out, beneath the river, the outline of a face. The more I gazed, the clearer it became: a young woman, observed from slightly above, squinting into bright light.

The restorer had spotted something else. On the back was a faint pencilled date and my aunt's initials. She had painted the portrait herself, and then, for reasons nobody witnessed and nobody can now explain, covered it with a bridge.

I have hung it where I catch sight of it every morning. I have left the river as it is.

ex.q: How did visitors treat the painting?
The restoration took three months.
What was hidden under the river?
o: A portrait of a young woman

ex.q: Who painted the hidden portrait?

l.intro: A guide and a visitor stand in front of a painting. The painting is invented.

script.t: Most people glance at this one and move on. What do you see?
A large, gloomy landscape. Dark green hills, a small white house. Nothing remarkable.
Stand where I am and look again. Don't stare at the house. Let your eyes wander.
There's something in the lower corner. I can just make out a figure.
Go on.
A tiny red-coated woman, walking away. I hadn't spotted her at all.
Almost nobody does. Now peer at the upstairs window.
There's a face. Somebody is watching her leave. That changes everything.
The painter observed that people see what they expect. A quiet landscape, so they scan it for trees.
And miss the story. How long have you been showing people this?
Twenty years. I still catch sight of things I hadn't noticed.

ex.q: How do most visitors react to the painting?
o: They study it for a long time
They look briefly and walk on

ex.q: The visitor notices the woman in the corner immediately.
What is at the upstairs window?
What does the guide say about herself?
